title: When police may arrest without warrant

content.overview: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Act 46 of 2023, is the current general criminal-procedure statute for proceedings governed by the post-1 July 2024 regime. Its central design is sequential: information, investigation, judicial scrutiny, charge, trial, judgment and remedies, with constitutional liberty and the s. 531 savings rule controlling the transition from the CrPC.
content.glance: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Act 46 of 2023, is the current general criminal-procedure statute for proceedings governed by the post-1 July 2024 regime. Its central design is sequential: information, investigation, judicial scrutiny, charge, trial, judgment and remedies, with constitutional liberty and the s. 531 savings rule controlling the transition from the CrPC.
content.study:
Statutory identity and commencement
The BNSS contains 531 sections in 39 chapters and replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for the new-law regime from 1 July 2024. It is procedural legislation. The offence is ordinarily identified under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 or another substantive statute, while proof is governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. A correct opinion keeps those three questions separate: what conduct is charged, what procedure applies, and how the facts may be proved.

The transition rule is not a footnote. Section 531(2)(a) preserves the CrPC for every appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending immediately before 1 July 2024. The first question in a file is therefore the relevant procedural status and date, not merely the date on which a later hearing occurred.

Procedural architecture
Chapter I supplies the preliminary provisions and definitions. The early chapters constitute criminal courts, prosecutors and police powers. The arrest and process chapters regulate liberty, summons, warrants, proclamation, search and seizure. Investigation provisions address information, statements, remand, case diaries, police reports and forensic duties. Later chapters govern cognizance, complaints, charges, the several forms of trial, evidence in inquiry and trial, judgment, appeals, revision, transfer, bail, maintenance, public order and the repeal and savings scheme.

The statutory sequence is a safeguard against arbitrary acceleration. Registration of information does not prove the accusation. Arrest does not establish guilt. A police report does not bind the Magistrate on cognizance. A charge is not a conviction. Each stage has its own threshold, forum and remedy.

High-value statutory checkpoints
1. Section 35: arrest without warrant, necessity and notice of appearance for the relevant lower-punishment cases.
2. Sections 43 and 47-58: manner of arrest, safeguards, grounds, intimation and production.
3. Section 105: audio-video recording of search and seizure, subject to the enacted conditions.
4. Section 173: information in cognizable cases, including electronic communication and the limited preliminary-enquiry route in s. 173(3).
5. Section 176(3): forensic visit and videography requirements for offences meeting the statutory punishment threshold, as brought into force and operationalised.
6. Section 187: remand and the statutory custody periods. Police custody must be argued from the enacted windows and judicial order, not from a memorised CrPC formula.
7. Sections 210 and 230: cognizance and supply of police papers and documents.
8. Sections 250-251 and 262-263: discharge and framing of charge at the relevant trial stages.
9. Sections 478-483: bailable bail, undertrial release, regular bail, anticipatory bail and higher-court bail powers. Section 482 is anticipatory bail; inherent powers are in s. 528.
10. Section 356: the statutory conditions for trial in absentia of a proclaimed offender.
11. Sections 413-445: appeals and revision, including the separate revision chapter.
12. Section 531: repeal and savings, which determines whether the CrPC remains the governing procedural code.

Courtroom and evidence discipline
The competent forum depends on the offence, the First Schedule or special statute, territorial rules, the stage of the proceeding and any statutory transfer or sanction requirement. Criminal limitation is not a single universal period: check the BNSS limitation provisions and the applicable special enactment. The Limitation Act, 1963 should not be mechanically substituted for a BNSS rule.

The prosecution bears the burden of proving the charge beyond reasonable doubt, subject to statutory presumptions and burdens that are lawfully engaged. BSA ss. 104-106 govern proof burdens; BSA s. 63 governs the statutory route for electronic records. A digital case diary, CCTV export, call record or device image must be analysed for relevance, authenticity, integrity and certificate requirements. Section 63 BSA does not cure an illegal search, an absent foundational fact or a failure to satisfy a BNSS condition precedent.

Constitutional foundation
Articles 14, 20, 21 and 22 inform the interpretation of criminal procedure. Fair investigation, non-arbitrary arrest, production before a Magistrate, legal representation, disclosure and a reasonably speedy trial are not decorative values. They control how statutory power is exercised. The remedy for a procedural breach depends on the provision, prejudice, seriousness of the violation and the order sought: release, bail, exclusion or weight, quashing, compensation, a fresh proceeding, disciplinary action or appellate correction may not be interchangeable.

Method for solving any BNSS problem
First identify the procedural stage and the date that activates either BNSS or the saved CrPC. Second identify the exact section and its conditions, provisos and connected provisions. Third identify the competent court and the available immediate remedy. Fourth map each fact to a statutory condition and state who bears the relevant burden. Fifth test electronic material under BSA s. 63 where applicable. Finally distinguish an irregularity from a jurisdictional or constitutional violation and state a precise order the court can grant. A current answer cites BNSS first and gives the CrPC number only as historical concordance when it assists comparison.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective and Constitutional Foundation
sections.body:
The BNSS is Act 46 of 2023 and commenced on 1 July 2024, subject to the repeal and savings scheme.
It codifies criminal procedure while preserving the constitutional requirements of equality, personal liberty, arrest safeguards and fair trial.
Its procedural stages must be kept distinct from BNS offences and BSA proof rules.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Chapters and Core Statutory Routes
sections.body:
Read the Act as a sequence from information and investigation through cognizance, charge, trial, judgment and appellate or revisional remedy.
The arrest, remand, bail, search, forensic, electronic communication and trial-in-absentia provisions must be read with their conditions and connected sections.
Section 482 is anticipatory bail; s. 528 contains the High Court inherent-power provision.

sections.heading: Mandatory Procedural Ingredients and Stage Tests
sections.body:
Identify the stage, the competent forum, territorial jurisdiction, statutory condition precedent and available remedy.
For arrest, test necessity and notice requirements; for remand, test custody period and judicial authorisation; for trial, test supply of documents, charge and evidence.
For every application, state the precise order sought rather than treating every defect as automatic acquittal or quashing.

sections.heading: BSA 2023 Evidentiary Burdens and Digital Records
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; s. 106 concerns facts especially within knowledge only after the legal foundation is laid.
BSA s. 63 must be checked for electronic records, including the identity of the device or system, production method and certificate requirements applicable to the record.
Admissibility, relevance, authenticity and probative weight are distinct questions. BSA compliance does not retrospectively validate an unlawful procedural step.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Transition
sections.body:
For post-1 July 2024 proceedings, cite the BNSS section and the First Schedule or special statute for classification and trial forum.
For a matter pending immediately before 1 July 2024, begin with s. 531(2)(a) and preserve the CrPC route unless a specific statutory rule changes the result.
Check the BNSS limitation provisions and special enactment before importing a Limitation Act period; calculate the remedy deadline from the actual order or event.

examples.title: Example 1 - Post-commencement proceeding
examples.body: A cognizable offence is reported on 15 August 2024. The police register information under BNSS s. 173, apply the arrest test under s. 35, seek any necessary remand under s. 187, and file the police report under the current BNSS route. A CCTV export is separately tested under BSA s. 63.

examples.title: Example 2 - Saved proceeding
examples.body: An investigation and trial were pending immediately before 1 July 2024. A later interlocutory hearing does not, by itself, convert the proceeding into a BNSS case. The advocate must begin with s. 531(2)(a) and identify the saved CrPC route.

hypotheticals.question: Which procedural code applies, whether the remand can be authorised, and how should the digital record be argued?
hypotheticals.analysis: 1. Identify the relevant procedural proceeding and the date on which it was pending, not merely the date of alleged conduct. 2. Apply s. 531(2)(a) only if the appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation was pending immediately before 1 July 2024; otherwise use the current BNSS route. 3. Test the remand request against s. 187, the custody window and the Magistrate's recorded reasons. 4. Separately test the phone extraction for relevance, foundation, authenticity and s. 63 BSA compliance. 5. State the remedy precisely: modification or refusal of custody, bail, direction for proper production, or another order supported by the proved defect.

distinctions.title: BNSS procedure vs BNS offence vs BSA proof

rows.right: What conduct is criminal and how facts are proved

rows.left: s. 531 savings controls pending procedural matters
rows.right: Date of offence and evidentiary law require separate analysis

rows.left: Wrong stage, forum, custody or remedy
rows.right: Wrong offence, missing ingredient, inadmissible or weak proof

misconceptions.trap: BNSS automatically governs every hearing held after 1 July 2024.
misconceptions.correction: Section 531(2)(a) preserves the CrPC for an appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending immediately before commencement. Determine the procedural status first.

misconceptions.trap: BNSS s. 482 contains the High Court inherent power.
misconceptions.correction: Section 482 is anticipatory bail. The inherent-power provision is s. 528.

misconceptions.trap: A police report proves the charge and a digital printout is automatically evidence.
misconceptions.correction: A police report is a procedural document and the charge remains to be proved. Electronic records require the applicable BSA s. 63 route and foundational proof.

cases.name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
cases.facts: The petitioner sought registration of information disclosing a cognizable offence.
cases.issue: Whether registration of an FIR is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Registration is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence; a limited preliminary inquiry is permissible only in the categories and manner recognised by the judgment.
cases.holding: The Constitution Bench directed compliance with mandatory registration subject to the limited preliminary-inquiry framework.
cases.relevance: Use with the current BNSS s. 173 information and preliminary-enquiry analysis.

cases.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
cases.facts: The case concerned arrest and detention for an offence carrying imprisonment up to seven years.
cases.issue: Whether arrest and remand may be authorised mechanically in a lower-punishment case.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Police must satisfy and record the necessity conditions for arrest, and Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically.
cases.holding: The Court issued directions to enforce the discipline associated with CrPC s. 41 and 41A, now read with the BNSS s. 35 framework.
cases.relevance: The leading constitutional safeguard for BNSS arrest analysis.

cases.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.facts: The Court addressed custodial violence and the absence of reliable arrest safeguards.
cases.issue: What minimum procedural protections must accompany arrest and detention.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Arrest and custody must be accompanied by transparent safeguards, documentation and accountability protecting Articles 21 and 22.
cases.holding: The Court prescribed arrest and custody safeguards that inform the statutory duties now found across the BNSS arrest provisions.
cases.relevance: Use for arrest memo, intimation, custody records and constitutional remedies.

cases.name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
cases.facts: Undertrial prisoners remained in custody for periods exceeding the possible sentence or without timely trial.
cases.issue: Whether prolonged criminal detention without a speedy trial violates Article 21.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The right to a speedy trial is part of Article 21 and requires the State to avoid unjustified, prolonged undertrial detention.
cases.holding: The Court directed attention to release and trial of undertrials and constitutional speed in criminal adjudication.
cases.relevance: Use with BNSS s. 479 undertrial release and the trial timeline provisions.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Provide a structured Case Brief and legal problem assessment on the BNSS 2023 framework.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE AND JURISDICTIONAL THRESHOLD
Identify the procedural stage, the relevant court, and whether the proceeding was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. Section 531(2)(a) is the first transition checkpoint.

II. GOVERNING RULE AND STATUTORY ANATOMY
For a post-commencement matter, cite the exact BNSS provision governing information, arrest, remand, bail, trial or remedy. Keep BNS liability and BSA proof analytically separate.

III. APPLICATION TO FACTUAL DISPUTE
Map each fact to the condition precedent. For arrest and remand, test necessity, notice, custody period and judicial reasons. For digital records, test relevance, foundation and BSA s. 63.

IV. CONCLUSION AND OPERATIVE ADVICE
State whether the order should be maintained, modified, set aside or followed by bail, further investigation, disclosure or another precise remedy.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: IRAC assessment for the current BNSS framework, with s. 531 transition and BSA digital-proof checkpoints.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Draft comprehensive Written Submissions on the BNSS framework, transition and evidence.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. STATEMENT OF FACTS AND PROCEDURAL PROVENANCE
Set out the registration date, procedural stage, orders passed, custody periods and the material relied upon.

II. STATUTORY SCHEME AND LEGISLATIVE INTENT
Explain the sequence from information and investigation to cognizance, charge, trial and remedy. Read each power with its liberty safeguard and identify the exact current BNSS section.

III. SATISFACTION OF MANDATORY PROCEDURAL INGREDIENTS
Address jurisdiction, notice or arrest necessity, remand limits, supply of papers, charge, trial stage and the relevant bail or appellate route.

IV. JUDICIAL PRECEDENTS AND RATIO DECIDENDI
Apply Lalita Kumari, Arnesh Kumar, D.K. Basu and Hussainara Khatoon only to the propositions they decide. Explain the statutory BNSS provision to which each principle is connected.

V. REBUTTAL OF ADVERSARY CONTENTIONS
Answer the s. 531 transition argument, any forum or limitation objection, and any challenge or defence concerning BSA s. 63 electronic records. Do not use s. 106 BSA to reverse the initial burden without foundational facts.

VI. PRAYER / RELIEF SOUGHT
Seek the exact procedural order supported by the record: refusal or modification of custody, bail, disclosure, direction for lawful investigation, quashing where maintainable, or appellate correction.

examTips: Start with the procedural date and s. 531 savings analysis.
Never confuse s. 482 anticipatory bail with s. 528 inherent powers.
Separate BNS charge, BNSS procedure and BSA proof in every answer.
Name the precise forum and operative remedy rather than merely alleging an irregularity.
revisionPoints: Section 531(2)(a) preserves the CrPC for specified matters pending immediately before commencement.
Sections 35, 173, 187, 480, 482, 528 and 531 are high-value current-law checkpoints.
BSA s. 63 governs electronic-record admissibility; BSA ss. 104-106 govern proof burdens.
Procedure, offence and proof are separate analytical layers.
